senses.gloss:
Mātṛkānighaṇṭu
(‘dictionary of Mātṛkās [or letters of the alphabet]’)
------------------------------------------
The tantras—religions works dealing mainly with the Devi-cult or worship of God as the Divine Mother—have exercised a tremendous influence over the ritualistic and the practical aspects of हिन्दुइस्म्. The upāsanā or meditation upon a deity also requires the जप (repetition) of the मन्त्र (name or an esoteric formula). This मन्त्र, more often than not, has a बीज or a seed-letter. There are different bījas for different deities of the Hindu pantheon. Also, the same बीज can represent several deities.
To keep the science well-guarded, but intelligible only to the initiates, the तन्त्रस् adopt a round-about way of indicating these bījas. Unless the methodology adopted is understood by the initiates, it is impossible to decipher these bījākṣaras or bījamantras.
To help the novitiates in this field, expert teachers have composed abhi-dhānas, kośas and nighaṇṭus (dictionaries) that unravel the mystic syllables more easily.
The following list gives some of these works, arranged in the English alphabetical order:
1. Bījābhidhāna (of Bhūtaḍāmaratantra)
This is a small work of 75 lines in anuṣṭubh metre describing the बीज-mantras like hrīm, strīm, aim, krīm representing various deities like Aindrī, Vāmekṣaṇā, सरस्वती and Kālī.
2. Bījanighaṇṭu (of भैरव)
The author भैरव says in the beginning of this work that it is based on the information given in the Bhūtaḍāmaratantra and the Śrutis he has studied.
It starts with the narration as to what the 50 letters of the alphabet stand for.
This is followed by various बीज-mantras like śrīṁ, ह्रीṁ, krīṁ, huṁ and others, and, what deities they represent.
3. Ekākṣarakośa (of Puruṣottamadeva)
As the very name indicates, this short work describes the various gods and goddesses as also other objects represented by each of the Sanskrit alphabets. For instance if ‘a’ represents वासुदेव, ‘ā’ stands for the Pitāmaha (Brahmā). ‘Pa’ indicates Pavana (god of wind). ‘Sā’ represents both लक्ष्मी and शिव.
4. Mantrābhidhāna
There are 35 ślokas in this work. This too describes the letters of the alphabet—called ‘mātṛkā-akṣaras’—as standing for certain deities.
5. Mantrārthābhidhāna (of Varadātantra)
This is a short work of 50 lines in the śloka metre. It describes the various bījamantras like hauṁ (for शिव), dūm (for दुर्गा), krīṁ (for Kālikā), ह्रीṁ (for भुवनेश्वरी), klīṁ (for Kāmadeva), gaṁ (for गणेश), kṣrauṁ (for नरसिṁह) and so on.
6. Mātṛkānighaṇṭu (of Mahīdāsa)
Like the other works described above, this work also describes in 59 verses the letters of the alphabet and what they stand for. For instance, ‘a’ stands for श्रीकण्ठ (Śiva), Keśava (Kṛṣṇa) and Vāta (god of wind). The letter ‘ka’ represents Māyā and Deveśa. If ‘ma’ denotes वैकुण्ठ (Viṣṇu) and महाकाल (Śiva), ‘ya’ stands for यमुना.
There are three more similar works which are variations of the ones already mentioned like the Mantrābhidhāna, with practically the same subject-content.

Mataṅga
------------------------------------------
A great sage classed among the brahmarṣis, he had his hermitage on the Ṛṣyamūka hill (near हम्पि in Karnataka). When वालि killed the demon दुन्दुभि and threw his severed head, it fell in this hermitage defiling it. The sage got angry and cursed that वालि would die if he ever stepped into this place.
Since सुग्रीव, the younger brother of वालि, knew this, he took shelter on this hillock along with his loyal ministers (including हनुमान्) to escape from वालि.
According to the legends connected with the exploits of ललिता (an aspect of पार्वती, spouse of Lord शिव), मतङ्ग was a great sage endowed with the knowledge and power of various mantras. His daughter Mātaṅgī was an attendant of ललिता.

mātā
(‘one who is honoured or worshipped’, ‘mother’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism has given the highest place of honour to the मोथेर्. In fact; the very etymological derivation on the word ‘mātā’ is ‘mānyate pūjyate yā sā’, ‘one who is honoured or worshipped’. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (1.11) advises the outgoing student of the गुरुकुल (forest academy run by the ṛṣis or sages) to look upon his मोथेर् as if she were God Himself. In this series of pithy teachings, she is placed above the ड़थेर् and the Vedic teacher.
In fact, the status of motherhood has been raised to the highest level by depicting even God, as the Divine मोथेर्, in later religious literature like the पुराणस् and the तन्त्रस्.
It is the bounden duty of the son to protect her and maintain her at all costs even if she were a sinner, reduced to the level of an outcaste.
One of the smṛtis (the Śaṅkhalikhita) gives an interesting piece of advice to a son that he should not normally take sides when the ड़थेर् and the मोथेर् are quarrelling. If at all, he should side with the मोथेर्!
The epics and the पुराणस् are full of eulogy of the मोथेर् and of instances (like that of the Pāṇḍavas) where the sons have served their मोथेर् devotedly.
They also warn that if a मोथेर् is deeply hurt and utters a curse, it can never be averted.
Even during the historical period there are several instances where the mothers have inspired and shaped the character of their sons and the latter’s gratitude towards them.

Matsyendranātha
------------------------------------------
The नाथ चुल्त् is one of the more obscure religious cults of शैविस्म् which gives primary importance to the practice of हठयोग and the attainment of occult powers.
The गुरु-paramparā or the tradition of gurus has a long list of 84 सिद्धस् or perfected beings. In this list, Matsyendra-nātha (or Mīnanātha) is shown as the founder and the first teacher, the second being Gorakṣanātha or गोरख्नाथ्. According to other lists, आदिनाथ (or शिव) is the first teacher, मत्स्येन्द्रनाथ being the second. He is said to have been born out of the womb of a matsya or mīna (fish), as a perfected being. This was possible because he accidentally happened to listen to the teachings of Lord शिव to पार्वती, even while he was in the womb of his मोथेर् (a fish).
Gorakṣanātha or गोरख्नाथ् was his chief disciple. However, the Bengali tradition treats it the other way, making गोरख्नाथ् the teacher and Matsyendra-nāth as his chief disciple.
Buddhist tradition in Nepal identifies him with Avalokiteśvara Padmapāṇi. In Tibet he is called Lūipā.
He probably belonged to the 12th century A. D. though some like to place him in the 7th. The Akulavīratantra is attributed to him as the author.
Not much is known of his life and works.
See also NĀTHA-CULT.

mātṛkāyantra
(‘esoteric drawing of mātṛkās or letters of the alphabets’)
------------------------------------------
A मन्त्र is a mystic formula which is generally used for upāsanā (worship and meditation) and जप (repetition). There are several ways of making a मन्त्र efficacious before actually using it. The first of it is called ‘janana’ or extrication of the letters of the मन्त्र from a specially drawn ‘yantra’ or mystical figure. This is the ‘mātṛkāyantra’.
It may be drawn either by the filaments of certain flowers or चन्दन (sandal-paste) or भस्म (holy ash used in the worship of शिव). The base is a plate of gold or silver or copper.
The यन्त्र consists of eight petals surrounded by a square with gates. In the centre there is a small circle and radial passages spread from it to the petals. All the letters of the Sanskrit alphabet are incorporated in it in a particular order.
The actual method of deriving the required मन्त्र from this यन्त्र should be personally learnt from the गुरु.

matsyayantra
------------------------------------------
In the epics and the पुराणस् we often come across very difficult tests laid down for the contestants who wanted to win the hands of the best of क्षत्त्रिय maidens. If it was lifting and stringing the Śivadhanus (the great bow of Lord शिव) in the case of सीता (king जनक’s daughter), it was the मत्स्ययन्त्र in the case of द्रौपदी, the Pāñcāla princess, the only daughter of the king Drupada.
The contrivance मत्स्ययन्त्र had a fish fixed near the roof of the big hall. Just below it, on the ground was a big pond full of oil. Between the two, nearer the roof, was a revolving disc containing a hole, the contestant had to discharge five arrows through the hole, while looking at the reflection of revolving wheel in the pond of oil, from the bow supplied, to hit the target fish.
Only अर्जुन succeeded in accomplishing this heroic and dexterous act. (Vide महाभारत, Ādiparva, chapter 184-188.)

Matsyapurāṇa
(‘Purāṇa related to the मत्स्यावतार [or Fish-इन्चर्नतिओन्]’)
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस्, as secondary scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्, have contributed a lot to spread of religion, culture and moral values as also several aspects of secular sciences like architecture or political science or health-care.
Out of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, the Matsyapurāṇa is considered not only important but also comparatively more ancient, assigned to the period circa A. D. 300.
The editions available in print now have 291 chapters and 14,000 verses.
It was probably a Vaiṣṇava work earlier, and, later additions might have been done by Śaivites, with a view to harmonising the two cults.
Many of the verses from the Vāyu and the Viṣṇudharmottara पुराणस् have been found here also. Hence it is difficult to say who has borrowed from whom.
Several dharmaśāstra works have quoted from this purāṇa profusely.
The purāṇa begins with a dialogue between lord विष्णु as the Matsya and मनु. Hence the name Matsyapurāṇa.
A brief account of the contents may be given as follows:
Creation of the world by ब्रह्मा and the Prajāpatis; destruction of Tripurāsura by शिव; सती’s immolation in दक्ष’s sacrifice; on कार्त्तिकेय; wars between the देवस् and असुरस्; geneologies of kings of the lunar and solar dynasties; names and accounts of future kings and races; avatāras of विष्णु (including the name of बुद्ध); ड़ुनेरल् रितेस्; vratas (religious vows and observances); दान (gifts); places of पिल्ग्रिमगे and bath in the holy rivers; वर्ण-आश्रम-dharmas; duties of women; establishing wells, tanks and gardens for public good; descriptions of hells; stories about the Śivaliṅgas.
See also PURĀṆAS.

mātṛkānyāsa
(‘keeping the mātṛkās [or the little mothers on the different parts of the body]’)
------------------------------------------
Ritualistic worship as also many rites associated with it are guided by the rules and regulations given in the आगमस् and the तन्त्रस्. One of the important acts in such rituals is the न्यास.
Literally ‘nyāsa’ means ‘keeping or placing’.
In मातृकान्यास, the various letters of the Sanskrit alphabet—considered as ‘mātṛkās’ or ‘little mothers’, aspects of the Divine Mother—are ceremonially placed on the different parts of the body, thus destroying the sins and purifying the same.
The ṛṣi (sage), छन्दस् (metre), devatā (deity) and बीज (seed) for this मातृकान्यास are, respectively, ब्रह्मा, गायत्री, Mātṛkādevī and all the letters of the alphabets.
Aṅganyāsa (also called ṣaḍaṅga-न्यास), antarmātṛkānyāsa and bahir-मातृकान्यास are the three aspects of this न्यास.
In all these, the letters of the alphabet adding anusvāra, ṁ, are used. For instance, in अङ्गन्यास: aṁ kaṁ khaṁ gaṁ ghaṁ ṅaṁ hṛdayāya namaḥ and so on.
In antarmātṛkānyāsa, the process concentrates on the six चक्रस् like स्वाधिष्ठान, maṇipūra up to ājñā with appropriate letters baṁ bhaṁ and so on.
In the bahirmātṛkānyāsa, the process of placing the letters is performed on the various limbs like the forehead, mouth, the eyes and so on.
There is also another न्यास called pīṭhanyāsa wherein the various शक्ति-pīṭhas are symbolically established on the different parts of the body thus purifying it.

Matsyāvatāra
(‘Fish-इन्चर्नतिओन्’)
------------------------------------------
This is the first of the दशावतारस् or Ten Incarnations of विष्णु. During this इन्चर्नतिओन् the Lord appeared as a tiny fish that fell into the hands of वैवस्वत मनु who was praying. When sheltered by him in his palace, he gradually grew into gigantic proportions instructing him to release him into the sea. There he told him how he would save him and the Saptarṣis—the Seven Sages—at the time of the great deluge destroying the world.
See also AVATĀRA and DAŚĀVATĀRAS.
